CausalChain: Chronic liver inflammation -> Activation of CAFs and alteration of LSECs -> Secretion of immunomodulatory cytokines (e.g., IL-6, CXCL11) -> Tumor cell production of immunosuppressive metabolites (kynurenine, SAM, MTA) and exosome-mediated transfer of ncRNAs -> Upregulation of PD-1/CTLA-4 on T cells and increased PD-L1 expression by LSECs -> Induction of T cell exhaustion and diminished cytotoxic responses -> Immunosuppressive TME supports tumor progression
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that an integrative intervention which simultaneously targets the metabolic pathways responsible for the production of immunosuppressive metabolites (kynurenine, SAM, and MTA) and disrupts exosomal ncRNA signaling in HCC will reprogram the tumor microenvironment to restore T cell functionality. Leveraging cutting-edge methodologies such as CRISPR-Cas9 screens, single-cell RNA sequencing, and metabolomic profiling, this dual-modality strategy is designed to intercept the cascade from chronic liver inflammation through stromal activation and cytokine release to eventual T cell exhaustion (via PD-1/PD-L1 and CTLA-4 upregulation). In combination with PD-1/PD-L1 immune checkpoint blockade, we expect that this comprehensive approach will synergistically reverse immunosuppression and promote robust antitumor immunity in HCC.
Abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is characterized by a complex interplay between chronic liver inflammation, stromal activation, altered cytokine secretion, and metabolic reprogramming that collectively establish an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). In our study, we propose an innovative, multi-targeted approach that couples the inhibition of metabolic pathways generating immunosuppressive metabolites—specifically, kynurenine, S-adenosylmethionine (SAM), and 5′-methylthioadenosine (MTA)—with disruption of exosome-mediated non-coding RNA signaling. Utilizing state-of-the-art technologies, including CRISPR-Cas9 screening, single-cell RNA sequencing, and advanced metabolomics, we will delineate the key nodes of the immunosuppressive cascade initiated by chronic inflammation. By reprogramming the TME to restore T cell functionality and combining this strategy with PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint inhibition, we aim to attenuate T cell exhaustion and enhance therapeutic efficacy in HCC. This integrative approach addresses multiple layers of tumor immune evasion and offers a novel, translatable strategy for improving HCC outcomes.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis proposed that inhibiting metabolic pathways in HCC cells to decrease production of specific immunosuppressive metabolites (kynurenine, SAM, and MTA) would reprogram the TME and work synergistically with PD-1/PD-L1 blockade. The revised hypothesis retains this core logic by targeting the same metabolic nodes but explicitly integrates additional mechanisms—namely, the role of exosomal ncRNA signaling—in the maintenance of an immunosuppressive TME. This revision enriches the causal chain by addressing the contribution of polyamine metabolism and paracrine signaling, providing a more comprehensive disruption of the immunosuppressive cascade. Furthermore, it leverages contemporary technologies (CRISPR screening, single-cell transcriptomics, advanced metabolomics) to enhance the strategic targeting and validation of each step in the causal chain: from inflammation-induced stromal activation and cytokine secretion, through the production and dissemination of immunosuppressive signals, to T cell exhaustion and tumor progression. This expanded and technologically informed approach offers improved practical implementability and translational potential.
